script.title: Married, one W-2 and one freelancer: how to handle the taxes
script.hook: If you're married and one of you has a regular job while the other freelances, your taxes work differently from what either of you is used to. The job's withholding doesn't cover the freelance income, the freelancer's tax rate is higher than it would be alone, and you have two different ways to pay during the year. In this video we'll work through one fictional couple with twenty twenty-six federal numbers, compare quarterly payments with extra withholding, and cover health insurance and retirement. Education, not advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: If you're married and one of you has a regular job while the other freelances, your taxes work differently from what either of you is used to. The job's withholding doesn't cover the freelance income, the freelancer's tax rate is higher than it would be alone, and you have two different ways to pay during the year. In this video we'll work through one fictional couple with twenty twenty-six federal numbers, compare quarterly payments with extra withholding, and cover health insurance and retirement. Education, not advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with two rings, a briefcase and a laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The couple
segments.narration: Meet Jordan and Riley, both fictional. Jordan works for a company and earns seventy thousand dollars in wages, with tax withheld from every paycheck. Riley freelances and expects forty thousand dollars of profit this year, after business expenses. They're married and file jointly, with the twenty twenty-six standard deduction of thirty-two thousand two hundred. No kids, no other income, to keep the math clear.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coin stacks side by side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: SE tax
segments.narration: Start with Riley's self-employment tax, because it's per person. It's fifteen point three percent on ninety-two point three five percent of Riley's profit: about five thousand six hundred fifty-two dollars. Jordan's salary doesn't change it. Jordan already pays Social Security and Medicare through payroll, and the Social Security wage limit applies to each person separately.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with a slice. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Income tax
segments.narration: Then income tax, on both incomes together. Add Jordan's wages and Riley's profit, subtract half of Riley's self-employment tax, the joint standard deduction, and the twenty percent qualified business income deduction on Riley's business income. Taxable income is about sixty-seven thousand five hundred. Income tax is about seven thousand six hundred nine. Total federal tax for the couple: about thirteen thousand two hundred sixty-one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a bill with two names. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The gap
segments.narration: Now, what does Jordan's employer withhold? It depends on Jordan's Form W-4, but say it matches the tax on Jordan's wages alone: about four thousand forty. Thirteen thousand two hundred sixty-one minus four thousand forty leaves about nine thousand two hundred twenty-one that nobody is paying yet. That's the tax caused by Riley's freelance income.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a bill with a slice missing. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Alone vs married
segments.narration: Here's the surprise. If Riley were single with the same forty thousand and no other income, federal tax would be about seven thousand four hundred twenty-seven. Married to Jordan, Riley's income causes about nine thousand two hundred twenty-one. That's eighteen point six percent alone versus twenty-three point one percent married. Jordan's wages fill the lowest brackets and most of the standard deduction, so every dollar of Riley's profit is taxed higher.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a bar chart with two bars. No text, no logos, no real people.

chart.title: Tax caused by Riley's $40K
chart.note: 2026 federal. Single vs married filing jointly. Fictional example.

segments.heading: The rule
segments.narration: The rule for paying during the year applies to the couple. If you'll owe a thousand dollars or more after withholding, you're expected to pay during the year. You generally avoid a penalty if withholding plus estimated payments cover the smaller of ninety percent of this year's tax, or a hundred percent of last year's joint tax. A hundred and ten percent if last year's adjusted gross income was over a hundred fifty thousand.
segments.on_screen_text: Smaller of 90% this year or 100% last
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shield. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Option 1
segments.narration: Option one: joint estimated payments. You use Form ten forty ES, both names and Social Security numbers, on the four due dates. For our couple, to reach ninety percent of this year's tax, they need about seven thousand eight hundred ninety-five beyond Jordan's withholding. That's about nineteen seventy-four a quarter. Riley sets aside a share of each client payment and pays from that.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four calendar pages. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Option 2
segments.narration: Option two: more withholding from Jordan's paycheck. Jordan gives the employer a new Form W-4 with an extra amount per paycheck in step four c. To cover the whole gap over twenty-six biweekly paychecks, that's about three hundred fifty-five per paycheck. To just reach the ninety percent mark, about three hundred four. No quarterly dates to remember, and nothing for Riley to send.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a paycheck with a plus sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The timing trick
segments.narration: Option two has a hidden advantage. Withholding is treated as paid evenly through the year, no matter when it actually came out. Quarterly payments count on the day you make them. So if a couple realizes in July that they've paid nothing, extra withholding for the rest of the year can cover the earlier quarters too. With thirteen paychecks left, that's about seven hundred ten each to cover the full gap.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four equal coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Trade-offs
segments.narration: The trade-off is cash flow and control. Withholding takes money from every paycheck whether Riley had a good month or a slow one. Estimated payments let you pay when the freelance money actually arrives. Many couples mix them: a fixed extra amount withheld to cover most of it, and a small top-up payment in April or January if Riley's year turns out bigger.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two arrows into one jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Tools
segments.narration: The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator on irs.gov handles exactly this situation: wages for one spouse and self-employment income for the other. It tells you what to put on the W-4. Run it at the start of the year, and again mid-year with real numbers. It takes about fifteen minutes with a recent pay stub and Riley's profit so far.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop with a simple form. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Health insurance
segments.narration: Health insurance changes too. If Riley could join Jordan's employer plan, and the employer pays part of it, Riley generally can't take the self-employed health insurance deduction for those months, even if Riley buys a separate plan. If Jordan's plan doesn't offer family coverage, or Riley isn't eligible, Riley's own premiums can be deductible, up to Riley's business profit.
segments.on_screen_text: Spouse's work plan? No SE health deduction
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a heart with a lock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Retirement
segments.narration: Retirement is per person. Jordan has the work 401(k) with its own deferral limit. Riley can open a SEP IRA or a Solo 401(k) on Riley's freelance income. At forty thousand of profit, a SEP allows about seven thousand four hundred thirty-five. Contributions lower the couple's income tax, which shrinks the gap a little, but not Riley's self-employment tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two piggy banks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three couples
segments.narration: The pattern holds at other incomes too. Fifty thousand of wages plus twenty-five thousand of freelance profit: the freelance income adds about five thousand six hundred twenty-three, twenty-two and a half percent. Ninety thousand plus sixty thousand: about thirteen thousand nine hundred ninety-two, twenty-three point three percent. For most of these couples, about twenty-three percent plus state tax is a sensible set-aside on the freelance profit.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three pairs of coin stacks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State
segments.narration: Don't forget your state. Most states with an income tax also want estimated payments or enough withholding, often on the same dates. The same two options usually work: extra state withholding on Jordan's state form, or joint state estimated payments. Check your state revenue department's site for its rules.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map outline with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Filing separately
segments.narration: Could filing separately help? Rarely, for a couple like this. Married filing separately uses narrower brackets, makes several credits unavailable, and lowers the safe-harbor income line to seventy-five thousand dollars per spouse. It can make sense in unusual situations, like income-driven student loan payments, so if that's you, run both ways in tax software before you file.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two forms, one crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Both freelance
segments.narration: And if you both freelance? Each of you has your own Schedule C and your own self-employment tax. You can still make joint estimated payments covering both businesses, and the set-aside works the same way: a share of every client payment, from both of you, into one tax savings account.
segments.on_screen_text: Both freelance: one joint tax jar
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two laptops and one jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Four mistakes couples make. Assuming the W-2 withholding covers everything. Using the solo-freelancer set-aside percentage, which is too low when you're married to a salary. Claiming the self-employed health deduction when the spouse's work plan was available. And forgetting to update the W-4 after a big change in either income.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four small warning signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Self-employment tax is per person. Income tax is joint, and the freelance income lands in a higher bracket because the salary fills the lower ones: about twenty-three percent for our couples, plus state. Cover the gap with joint estimated payments, extra withholding through the W-2 spouse's W-4, or both. Withholding counts as paid evenly, which makes it a good catch-up tool. Check health insurance eligibility and give the freelancer their own retirement account. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes closing a notebook and smiling. No text, no logos, no real people.
